introduction-the-amnesia-patient.core: Every cloud VM boots from a generic image that knows nothing about itself: not its hostname, SSH keys, users, packages or role. cloud-init runs at first boot, reads instance metadata and user-data from the cloud's metadata service or a config drive, and configures the machine: network, users and keys, files, packages, commands. It's how one golden image becomes many differently configured servers.

first_principles.problem: Every new VM requires an engineer to SSH in and configure users, packages and services by hand.

analogy.title: A new employee reading their welcome pack
analogy.story: They arrive knowing nothing, read the pack (user-data), and set up their desk, accounts and tools accordingly.
analogy.breaks: Employees remember; cloud-init tracks state by instance ID.

code.text:
#cloud-config
hostname: web-01
users:
  - name: deploy
    ssh_authorized_keys: ["ssh-ed25519 AAAA... deploy@ci"]
    sudo: "ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL"
packages: [nginx]
runcmd:
  - systemctl enable --now nginx

check.q: Where does cloud-init get instance-specific information on AWS?
check.a: From the EC2 instance metadata service (IMDS) at 169.254.169.254, including user-data.

user-data-vs-cloud-config.core: User-data is whatever you pass at launch, and cloud-init detects its type by the first line. #cloud-config means declarative YAML handled by modules; #!/bin/bash (or any #!) means a shell script run once late in boot; #include means a list of URLs; multi-part MIME combines several parts; and Jinja templates (## template: jinja) can use instance data. Prefer cloud-config for idempotent, readable configuration and use scripts for the rest.

first_principles.problem: A bash user-data script partially fails on rerun and leaves the VM half-configured.
truths: The first line decides the format.

analogy.title: A checklist vs a handwritten set of instructions
analogy.story: A checklist (cloud-config) is easy to read and verify; free-form instructions (scripts) are flexible but error-prone.
analogy.breaks: Checklists don't execute; cloud-config modules do.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Declarative base plus a custom script.

check.q: How does cloud-init know whether user-data is cloud-config or a script?
check.a: By its first line: '#cloud-config' for YAML config, '#!' for an executable script.

cloud-config-syntax-essentials.core: Common cloud-config keys: users and groups (with ssh_authorized_keys, sudo, shell), packages, package_update and package_upgrade, write_files (path, content, permissions, owner, encoding), runcmd (commands late in boot) versus bootcmd (every boot, very early), mounts and disk_setup, ntp, timezone, and power_state for reboot. YAML is strict about indentation, and keys are processed by modules in a fixed order, not the order you write them.

first_principles.problem: A runcmd that starts a service runs before write_files places its config file, or so the engineer assumes.
truths: Modules run in a defined order.
derivation: Use **packages** instead of apt in runcmd.

analogy.title: An assembly line with fixed stations
analogy.story: You hand over all the parts at once, but they're installed in the line's order, not the order you listed them.
analogy.breaks: Assembly lines are visible; module order lives in /etc/cloud/cloud.cfg.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Files written before runcmd reloads nginx.

code.text:
#cloud-config
package_update: true
packages: [nginx]
write_files:
  - path: /etc/nginx/conf.d/app.conf
    permissions: '0644'
    content: |
      server { listen 80; location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080; } }
runcmd:
  - [systemctl, reload, nginx]
# validate: cloud-init schema --config-file user-data.yaml

check.q: What's the difference between bootcmd and runcmd?
check.a: bootcmd runs very early on every boot; runcmd runs once per instance late in the first boot.

the-boot-stages-timing-is-everything.core: cloud-init runs in stages tied to systemd. Detect (ds-identify) finds the datasource; Local runs before networking to apply network config; Network runs after networking to fetch user-data and process disks, mounts and bootcmd; Config runs config modules (users, write_files and the like); Final runs late, after other services, doing package installs, runcmd and user scripts. Knowing which stage a module runs in explains ordering and timing bugs.

first_principles.problem: A user script tries to reach a database before networking and DNS are ready, and fails intermittently.

analogy.title: Opening a shop in the morning
analogy.story: Unlock doors and turn on power (local), connect phones and internet (network), set up displays (config), then open to customers (final).
analogy.breaks: Shop staff adapt; stages are fixed sequences.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: See which stage and module took time.

code.text:
cloud-init status --wait --long
cloud-init analyze show | head -20
cloud-init analyze blame | head
# Finished stage: (modules-final) 42.1 seconds — package installs dominate

check.q: In which cloud-init stage do runcmd and package installation happen?
check.a: The final stage, late in boot after networking and most services are up.

debugging-reading-the-logs.core: When cloud-init misbehaves, check cloud-init status --long for the overall result and errors; /var/log/cloud-init.log for detailed module execution with tracebacks; /var/log/cloud-init-output.log for stdout and stderr of scripts and runcmd; /run/cloud-init/ and /var/lib/cloud/instance/ for the rendered user-data, datasource and per-instance state; and cloud-init query to see metadata as cloud-init sees it. cloud-init clean lets you re-run on the next boot for testing.

first_principles.problem: Packages weren't installed on a new VM and there's no obvious error.
truths: Script output goes to a separate log.

analogy.title: A flight's black box and cabin recording
analogy.story: One records system events (cloud-init.log); the other records what was said (output.log).
analogy.breaks: Black boxes survive crashes; logs vanish if the instance is terminated.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Root cause: missing package index refresh.

code.text:
cloud-init status --long
# status: error  errors: ['Failed to install packages: [nginx]']
grep -n -A5 'WARNING\|Traceback' /var/log/cloud-init.log | head -30
tail -50 /var/log/cloud-init-output.log
# E: Unable to locate package nginx → package_update was false

check.q: Which log contains the stdout/stderr of runcmd and user scripts?

debugging-the-black-box-cant-ssh-in.core: If cloud-init broke SSH (bad user, wrong key, firewall, network config), you can't log in to read logs. Use out-of-band access instead: the serial or console output (aws ec2 get-console-output, which shows cloud-init and kernel messages), an interactive serial console (EC2 Serial Console, GCP serial port), SSM Session Manager if the agent runs, or as a last resort detach the root volume and attach it to a rescue instance to read /var/log.

first_principles.problem: A typo in user-data's ssh_authorized_keys locks everyone out of a new instance.

analogy.title: Locked out of the house
analogy.story: Peek through the window (console log), use the back door (serial console), or have a locksmith take the lock to a workshop (rescue instance).
analogy.breaks: Houses are worth rescuing; cloud instances are often just replaced.

code.text:
aws ec2 get-console-output --instance-id i-0abc123 --latest --output text | grep -i -E 'cloud-init|ci-info|error' | tail -20
# ci-info: no authorized SSH keys fingerprints found for user deploy.
# → key YAML was mis-indented

check.q: How can you see cloud-init output on an EC2 instance you can't SSH into?
check.a: Retrieve the console output with aws ec2 get-console-output, or use the EC2 Serial Console.
